name: Limatola Castle
architectural_style: Norman-origin 12th-century fortification over an earlier Lombard watchtower; expanded in 1277 under Charles I of Anjou; later held by the Della Ratta counts; restored and reopened as a hotel in 2010
visit_duration: Overnight stay; the restaurant, in the former stables, is separately open to the public
accessibility: All 30 rooms are within the historic castle; contact the hotel directly regarding specific accessibility requirements.
tagline: A Norman fortress expanded by Charles I of Anjou in 1277 — 30 rooms within the historic castle, a short drive from the Royal Palace of Caserta
highlights: Norman origin in the 12th century, one of the oldest militarily-founded castles in this Italian list
Expanded by Charles I of Anjou in 1277, a direct link to the Angevin conquest of southern Italy
Restaurant installed in the castle's historic stables
A short drive from the Royal Palace of Caserta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site
description:
Limatola Castle originated in the 12th century, when the Normans built a fortification over the remains of an earlier Lombard watchtower, taking advantage of an elevated position overlooking the surrounding valley in what is now Campania. In 1277, under the reign of Charles I of Anjou — the French monarch who took control of the Kingdom of Sicily following the Battle of Benevento — the castle was expanded and reinforced as part of the network of Angevin fortresses across southern Italy.

Over time it passed to the Della Ratta counts, one of the most influential feudal families in medieval and Renaissance Campania, who gradually transformed it from a military fortress into a noble residence. After centuries of continuous use and a long period of partial abandonment, the castle underwent a comprehensive restoration completed in 2010 by the Sgueglia family, who reopened it as a hotel while preserving the layout and much of the fortress's original fabric.

The Lombard watchtower beneath the Norman fortification points to an even earlier strategic use of this hilltop, a pattern common across southern Italy where later medieval castles frequently built over earlier early-medieval defensive structures.

Charles I of Anjou's 1277 expansion ties Limatola directly to one of the pivotal moments in southern Italian history — the transfer of power from the Hohenstaufen to the Angevin dynasty following the Battle of Benevento in 1266.

The Della Ratta family's long stewardship reflects the broader pattern of Campania's feudal nobility gradually converting military strongholds into residences as the region's defensive needs diminished under stable centralized rule.

The castle's proximity to the Royal Palace of Caserta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the largest royal residences in the world, gives guests staying at Limatola an easy full-day pairing between a night in a medieval fortress and a visit to a Bourbon royal palace.

faqs.question: Are all the rooms at Limatola Castle within the historic building?
faqs.answer: Yes — all 30 rooms are within the castle itself. The historic stables are used exclusively as the restaurant, with no guest rooms in that outbuilding.

faqs.question: Can I eat at Limatola Castle's restaurant without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes — the restaurant, housed in the castle's former stables, welcomes outside diners, not just hotel guests.

faqs.question: What is Limatola Castle close to?
faqs.answer: The Royal Palace of Caserta, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is about 30 minutes away — a natural pairing of a night at the castle with a full day at the royal palace.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** About 30 minutes from Caserta and 45 minutes from Naples by car; Naples' Capodichino Airport (NAP) is about 50 minutes away.

**Rooms & rates:** 30 rooms, all within the historic castle. From €112/night.

**On-site:** Restaurant in the former stables, gardens, event and wedding space.

**Good to know:** A short distance from the Royal Palace of Caserta (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) — a natural pairing of a night at the castle with a full day at the royal palace.

**Combine with:** The Royal Palace of Caserta (~30 min), Caserta Vecchia (a hilltop medieval village, ~35 min), Naples and the Campania coast.
